concepts.topicTitle: Pillars of Personal Finance and Budgeting
concepts.label: Personal Finance and Its Five Pillars
concepts.cardText: We earn income and spend it to fulfil our needs and wants, and we save and invest to achieve goals such as buying a house or funding higher education. Because money is an important resource that should be used efficiently, personal finance matters. Personal finance is the planning and management of an individual's money to meet their needs and wants: how much to spend, how much to save, where to invest and how to prepare for future needs. It rests on five pillars. Income is money received regularly or occasionally for products sold or services rendered, such as a salary, business profit, rent, interest or dividends; it is the starting point because without income one cannot spend, save or invest. Budgeting decides how income is spent on needs and wants. Saving sets money aside for future needs or emergencies. Investing deploys savings in assets such as stocks and mutual funds. Protection and risk management safeguards money and assets through insurance and debt management.

concepts.topicTitle: Pillars of Personal Finance and Budgeting
concepts.label: Budgeting: Planning How Income Will Be Spent
concepts.cardText: Budgeting means planning in advance how income will be spent. A budget is a written plan that aims to balance income and expenses, for example a family deciding how much to save each month and how much to spend on food, rent, school fees and transport. Setting financial goals, such as saving for a school trip, sports equipment, higher education or emergencies, helps people prioritise needs and make careful choices; a simple way is to ask what you want to achieve, how much money you need, by when, and what steps will help. Budgeting controls unnecessary spending such as excessive eating out or impulse shopping, enables people to prioritise important expenses and helps them live within their means. The steps are: identify your expenses, set a savings goal (for example, saving ₹3,000 in six months for a bicycle needs ₹500 a month), track your spending against the budget, and review and adjust the budget as income, expenses or goals change.

concepts.topicTitle: Saving, Investing, and the Power of Compounding
concepts.label: Saving and Investing: Protecting and Growing Money
concepts.cardText: Saving means keeping aside a part of one's income for future use; it is a financial surplus built up over time. Savings matter for comfortable living and because life is uncertain and emergencies can arise at any time; people also save to make later investments. Investing means putting savings into assets with the aim of protecting their value and generating returns. Priya keeps her ₹500 in a piggy bank and a year later still has ₹500, while Sameer puts his into a scheme earning 8% a year and has ₹540: both are being responsible, but they are not doing the same thing. Cash gives greater liquidity, but investing helps increase wealth and lets money grow faster than inflation, the rise in prices over time that reduces purchasing power. If a ₹1,000 school bag rises 6% a year it costs about ₹1,060 next year; money kept at home that does not grow can no longer buy it.

concepts.topicTitle: Saving, Investing, and the Power of Compounding
concepts.label: Compounding and the Advantage of Investing Early
concepts.cardText: Compounding is the principle where returns are earned not only on the original investment (the principal) but also on the returns already earned, so that high returns accumulate over time; it is the process in which an investment's earnings, such as interest or dividends, are reinvested to generate their own additional earnings. Take Bhavisha and Dhruv, who each save ₹1,000 at the end of every year and earn 7% annual interest. The only difference is that Bhavisha starts at 25 and Dhruv at 35. Although both save the same amount each year, by 65 Dhruv has only about 40% as much money as Bhavisha (about ₹94,460 against ₹1,99,635). Compounding lets earlier investments earn returns for a longer period, and those returns continue to generate more returns, which is why the growth curve is flat at first and steeper later.

concepts.label: Common Investment Options
concepts.cardText: Common investment options include fixed deposits, bonds, stocks and mutual funds. A fixed deposit (FD) is among the most common and safest options offered by banks and post offices: a lump sum is deposited for a fixed period, such as one, three or five years, and earns a fixed rate of interest that stays unchanged, giving assured returns suited to people who prefer safety over high returns. Government-backed options include the Public Provident Fund, the National Savings Certificate and the Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana. Bonds are lending to the government or companies for a fixed period for regular interest; a ₹10,000 bond at 5% pays ₹500 a year and government bonds are generally safer than corporate bonds. Shares represent ownership in a company and may earn returns through dividends and rising share prices; they carry higher risk because prices fluctuate, but have the potential for higher long-term returns. Mutual funds pool money from many investors into a basket of shares, bonds or other assets run by professional fund managers; they reduce risk through portfolio diversification.

concepts.label: Risk, Return, Time Horizon and Liquidity
concepts.cardText: When deciding where to invest, four factors matter: risk (the chance of losing money), return (the profit earned from an investment), time horizon (how long money can remain invested) and liquidity (how easily an asset can be converted into cash when needed). Different investments score differently: fixed deposits are generally low-risk, with steady but relatively lower returns; mutual funds may offer higher returns; and shares have the potential for the highest returns over the long term but also the highest risk. In general, lower-risk investments tend to offer lower returns, while higher-risk investments may offer higher returns, which is the risk-return trade-off. People should therefore choose investments based on their financial goals, the amount of risk they are willing to take and when they are likely to need the money.

concepts.topicTitle: Risk Protection, Insurance, and Responsible Credit
concepts.label: Insurance: Protection Through Risk Sharing
concepts.cardText: Life is full of uncertainties such as illness, accidents, loss of income or damage to property, and these can cause significant financial losses. Protection, safeguarding income, savings and assets against such risks, is therefore an important part of personal finance, and insurance is one of the most effective ways to achieve it. Insurance is a legal contract in which an individual pays a regular amount, called a premium, to an insurance company, which in return agrees to provide financial compensation for specific losses or expenses covered under the policy. It works on risk sharing: many people pay premiums into a common pool, and those who suffer an unexpected loss receive support. Types include health insurance (medical expenses; Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY covers eligible low-income households), life insurance (support for dependents if the policyholder passes away) and general insurance (vehicles, homes, businesses and other property, including motor, property, crop and cattle insurance).

concepts.topicTitle: Risk Protection, Insurance, and Responsible Credit
concepts.label: Borrowing, Credit and EMIs
concepts.cardText: Sometimes people need to borrow money from banks, relatives or other sources as loans. Borrowing or using credit can be helpful when used for productive purposes, but harmful if misused: an education loan can help a student pursue higher education, whereas borrowing to buy unnecessary consumer goods may lead to a debt burden and financial difficulties. Responsible borrowing means taking loans only when necessary and ensuring they can be repaid on time. An EMI (equated monthly instalment) is the fixed amount a person pays every month to repay a loan, and each EMI includes part of the original loan (the principal) as well as the interest charged by the lender. For example, a family buying a ₹30,000 refrigerator may repay it through an EMI of ₹3,000 for 12 months. Too many EMIs can affect savings and emergency funds.

concepts.topicTitle: Taxation and Personal Income Tax in India
concepts.label: Taxes: Direct, Indirect and Progressive
concepts.cardText: Taxes are compulsory payments made by individuals and businesses to the government to fund public services such as schools, hospitals, transport, defence and other essential facilities. There are two main types: direct taxes, paid directly on a person's or organisation's income or profits, such as income tax, and indirect taxes, added to the price of goods and services, such as the Goods and Services Tax (GST). Personal income tax is a tax paid on the income a person earns in a financial year, and all citizens of India with a personal income must pay it, except those earning below a certain limit. As income increases the tax payable also increases: this is progressive taxation, which aims to reduce income inequality by imposing higher rates on higher incomes, because people with greater financial capacity can afford to contribute more towards public services. Paying taxes honestly and on time is an important responsibility of every citizen.

concepts.topicTitle: Taxation and Personal Income Tax in India
concepts.label: Tax Slabs and Calculating Income Tax
concepts.cardText: India follows a slab system for income tax: taxable income is divided into ranges, called tax slabs, and each slab is taxed at a specified rate. The slabs are proposed by the Ministry of Finance as part of the Union Budget presented to Parliament every year, and the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT), under the Ministry of Finance, administers the laws relating to direct taxes. Under the New Tax Regime for FY 2025-26, income up to ₹4 lakh is taxed at nil, then 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25% and 30% above ₹24 lakh. Take Priya, who earns ₹14 lakh a year. After a standard deduction of ₹75,000 her taxable income is ₹13,25,000. Different portions of income are taxed at different rates: nil on the first ₹4 lakh, 5% of the next ₹4 lakh is ₹20,000, 10% of the next ₹4 lakh is ₹40,000 and 15% of the remaining ₹1,25,000 is ₹18,750, so her total tax is ₹78,750.
